newsitem.title: USA: U.S. spot gas prices surge on cold Midwest weather.
newsitem.headline: U.S. spot gas prices surge on cold Midwest weather.

text.p: U.S. spot natgas prices surged past the $3 per mmBtu mark Monday, as wintry cold temperatures blanketed the Midwest and were forecast to spread to other areas later this week, sources said.
Swing Gulf Coast prices were up nearly $1 to the $3.44-3.50 range, narrowing the discount to January indices to about 40 cents.
An arctic air mass is forecast to land in the Midwest and southern plains by Thursday, dragging temperatures as much as 25 degrees Fahrenheit below normal, the National Weather Service reported.

At the New York city-gate, where temperatures were normal to slightly below-normal, prices were carried higher by the stronger Gulf values. Traders said deals were mostly done around $4, up about 50 cents from Friday.
In the Appalachian region, prices jumped into the $3.50s and $3.60s, up about 70 cents from Friday.

The major factor contributing to the sharp price rise were the below-normal temperatures now in the Midwest. As a result, prices were up by the largest margin to the $3.40-3.75 area, as compared with Friday's range of $2.30-2.40.
Chicago city-gate values were talked in the $3.75-3.80 range.
A cold front is forecast to arrive to the Midwest Thursday, pressuring temperatures as much as 25 degrees below-normal.
The blast of cold air is also expected to spread into the southern plains later this week.
In west Texas, Permian gas prices gained more than $1 to the low-$3.60s. The cold front will likely push temperatures to at least 10 degrees below-normal in Texas, the NWS reported.
Texas Utilities shut its 1,150 megawatt Comanche Peak 2 nuclear unit this weekend. The company said it would likely restart late Tuesday or early Wednesday.
At the southern California border, prices soared to about $3.90, up about $1.40 from Friday.
Southern California Edison reported that strong winds in the area led to about 75,000 power outages to its customers.
